description: Calculating and interpreting PED and PES, the determinants of elasticity, and why it matters to firms and government.
content_html:
Why Doesn’t a Price Rise Always Cut Demand by the Same Amount?

When a petrol station puts its prices up by 10%, most drivers still fill their tanks — they have little choice. But when a cinema raises ticket prices by 10%, some people decide to stay home or stream instead. The quantity demanded falls more sharply. This difference in how sensitive quantity demanded is to a price change is captured by the concept of price elasticity of demand (PED).

PED tells producers and governments something vital: if you raise the price of this good, how much will demand fall? The answer determines whether total revenue goes up or down, and whether a tax will raise money or simply cause people to stop buying the good altogether.

Calculating PED

The formula is straightforward:

PED = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price

Percentage change is always calculated as: (change ÷ original value) × 100. So if the price of a cinema ticket rises from £10 to £12 (a 20% rise) and weekly admissions fall from 500 to 400 (a 20% fall), then PED = −20% ÷ 20% = −1. The answer is almost always negative because a price rise causes a fall in quantity demanded — they move in opposite directions. For simplicity, the negative sign is usually ignored and only the absolute value (the number without its sign) is compared.

Key Fact

PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. When PED is greater than 1 (ignoring the minus sign), demand is elastic — a price rise causes a proportionally bigger fall in quantity demanded. When PED is less than 1, demand is inelastic — a price rise causes a proportionally smaller fall in quantity demanded.

Elastic and Inelastic Demand

If PED = 2, a 10% price rise leads to a 20% fall in quantity demanded — demand is price elastic. Consumers are very sensitive to the price change. If PED = 0.3, a 10% price rise leads to only a 3% fall in quantity demanded — demand is price inelastic. Consumers barely change their behaviour. A PED of exactly 1 is called unit elastic — a 10% price rise causes a 10% fall in quantity demanded.

Availability of substitutes. The more substitutes a good has, the easier it is for consumers to switch away when the price rises, so demand is more elastic. Branded cola has close substitutes (own-brand cola, other soft drinks), so its demand is relatively elastic. Insulin for diabetics has no close substitute, so demand is highly inelastic.

Necessity versus luxury. Necessities like bread, heating, or prescription medicines have inelastic demand because consumers need them regardless of price. Luxuries like designer handbags or foreign holidays have more elastic demand — if the price rises sharply, consumers can simply go without or choose a cheaper option.

Proportion of income. When a good takes up a large share of a consumer’s income (a car, a house), even a small percentage price change feels significant, so demand tends to be more elastic. When the good costs very little (a box of matches, a bus timetable), consumers barely notice a price rise and demand is inelastic.

Time period. Demand becomes more elastic over time. In the short run, a driver who faces rising petrol prices has little choice but to pay — they still need to get to work. Over time, they might buy a more fuel-efficient car, move closer to work, or switch to public transport. The longer the time period, the more substitutes and adaptations become available.

PED and Total Revenue

The link between PED and total revenue (price × quantity sold) is one of the most useful applications of elasticity. Whether a price rise increases or decreases total revenue depends entirely on whether demand is elastic or inelastic.

If demand is inelastic (PED < 1): a price rise leads to only a small fall in quantity demanded, so total revenue rises. For example, a firm selling a necessity can raise its price by 20% and lose only 5% of its sales — revenue goes up. This is why governments tax petrol, alcohol and cigarettes so heavily: demand is inelastic, so the tax raises significant revenue without destroying sales.

If demand is elastic (PED > 1): a price rise leads to a proportionally bigger fall in quantity demanded, so total revenue falls. A firm that raises the price of a luxury good with many substitutes will find that so many customers switch away that its total income drops. In this case, cutting prices would actually increase total revenue because the gain in quantity more than offsets the lower price per unit.

Key Fact

PED and total revenue rule: inelastic demand (PED < 1) — a price rise increases total revenue. Elastic demand (PED > 1) — a price rise decreases total revenue. Firms use this to decide whether to raise or lower prices to maximise income.

Price Elasticity of Supply

Supply has its own elasticity measure. Price elasticity of supply (PES) tells us how readily producers can expand (or contract) output when the price changes:

PES = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price

Unlike PED, PES is positive — a higher price gives producers an incentive to supply more, so both quantity supplied and price move in the same direction. If PES = 3, a 10% price rise causes a 30% increase in quantity supplied: supply is elastic. If PES = 0.2, a 10% price rise causes only a 2% increase in supply: supply is inelastic.

Spare capacity. A factory with spare capacity can quickly increase output when prices rise, so its supply is relatively elastic. A factory already at full capacity cannot easily produce more in the short run, making supply inelastic.

Stocks and storage. If a firm holds large stocks of finished goods, it can respond quickly to a price rise by releasing stock onto the market — supply is elastic. Goods that cannot be stored (fresh strawberries, live concerts) have inelastic supply because output cannot be easily scaled up.

Ease of switching production. Firms that can easily redirect their resources to produce a different good respond quickly to price signals — supply tends to be more elastic. A specialist defence manufacturer cannot easily switch to making consumer electronics, so its supply of its original product is inelastic.

Time period. Supply becomes more elastic over time, just as demand does. In the short run, a housebuilder cannot immediately put up hundreds more homes just because house prices have risen. Over several years, land can be bought, planning permission granted, and new homes built. Supply in the long run is almost always more elastic than in the short run.

Implications for Producers and Government

Understanding both PED and PES matters for real decisions. A firm setting prices needs to know whether its customers are sensitive to price changes. A coffee shop in a high street with five competitors will face elastic demand — cutting its prices slightly could attract many more customers and raise total revenue. A utility company supplying water faces highly inelastic demand and operates as a natural monopoly — consumers cannot switch supplier, and there is no effective competition. This monopoly structure, compounded by inelastic demand (which would allow an unregulated monopolist to raise prices sharply), is exactly why the government regulates water prices rather than leaving them to the market.

Governments rely on inelastic demand when taxing goods like fuel, tobacco and alcohol. The tax raises prices, but because demand is inelastic, the quantity sold barely falls — tax revenue flows in reliably. However, the government also knows that a tax on a good with elastic demand (a luxury item with many substitutes) would cause sales to collapse, raising little revenue and harming the industry.

On the supply side, PES matters when a price signal reaches a market. If supply is inelastic — as it is for housing in areas of high demand — a sharp rise in house prices may not quickly attract enough new supply to bring prices back down. That is why housing markets can remain expensive for many years even when demand is strong.
exam_tip_html: The command word Calculate means you must show your working: write the formula first (PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price), calculate each percentage change, substitute, and give the answer. Do not just write the final number — you earn a mark for method even if your arithmetic slips. For Explain questions on elasticity, build a chain of reasoning: “The good has many substitutes, so demand is elastic; therefore, a price rise causes a proportionally larger fall in quantity demanded, so total revenue falls.” Common error: students say a firm should “raise prices to earn more revenue” without checking whether demand is elastic or inelastic — always link the pricing decision to the PED value first.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • PED measures how sensitive quantity demanded is to a price change (formula: % ΔQd ÷ % ΔP). Elastic demand (PED > 1) means consumers respond strongly; inelastic demand (PED < 1) means they barely react. Key determinants are availability of substitutes, necessity versus luxury, share of income, and time.
  • Elasticity links directly to total revenue: a price rise increases revenue when demand is inelastic, but decreases it when demand is elastic. Governments use inelastic demand to raise reliable tax revenue from goods like fuel and tobacco.
  • PES measures how readily producers adjust supply to a price change (formula: % ΔQs ÷ % ΔP). Key determinants are spare capacity, stockholding, ease of switching production, and time. Supply is almost always more elastic in the long run than in the short run.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following goods is most likely to have price inelastic demand?
A) A luxury foreign holiday
B) Designer trainers
C) Insulin for diabetics
D) Cinema tickets
practice_questions.marks: C) Insulin for diabetics [1 mark]. Insulin is a medical necessity with no close substitute; consumers must buy it regardless of price changes.

practice_questions.text:
The price of a coffee shop's flat white rises from £3.00 to £3.60. As a result, weekly sales fall from 800 cups to 680 cups.

Calculate the price elasticity of demand. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for the correct method/formula:
PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price
% change in Qd = (680 − 800) ÷ 800 × 100 = −15%
% change in price = (3.60 − 3.00) ÷ 3.00 × 100 = +20%
PED = −15 ÷ 20 = −0.75 (accept 0.75 ignoring the sign)
1 mark for the correct answer of −0.75 (or 0.75).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the availability of substitutes affects price elasticity of demand.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for stating that more substitutes make demand more elastic.
1 mark for developing: if a firm raises its price, consumers can switch to a close substitute, so quantity demanded falls by a proportionally larger amount.
1 mark for a relevant example or further development: for instance, branded cola faces competition from own-brand alternatives, so even a small price rise causes many buyers to switch, giving a PED greater than 1.

practice_questions.text: A supermarket sells a popular own-brand cereal. Its price elasticity of demand is 0.4. Explain how this information should influence the supermarket's pricing decision.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying that PED = 0.4 means demand is price inelastic (PED < 1).
1 mark for developing: a price rise will cause a proportionally smaller fall in quantity demanded.
1 mark for linking to total revenue: because the percentage fall in quantity sold is smaller than the percentage rise in price, total revenue will increase.
1 mark for a further developed point: the supermarket should therefore raise the price of this cereal to increase its revenue, as long as competitors do not undercut it significantly.

practice_questions.text: Analyse how price elasticity of demand affects a government's decision to impose a tax on a good such as fuel.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained chain of reasoning that connects inelastic demand to reliable tax revenue, with a well-developed explanation of why the tax raises prices by less than its full value if demand has any elasticity, and a clear link to the implication for both government revenue and consumer welfare. May also note limits (e.g. at very high tax levels even inelastic demand eventually weakens).

Secure (3–4 marks): Clear explanation that a tax on a good with inelastic demand raises prices but causes only a small fall in quantity, so revenue is substantial. Some development of the chain but analysis may not be fully sustained or may lack a clear link to implications.

Developing (2 marks): Some relevant points — for example, identifying that the government targets goods with inelastic demand — but the chain of reasoning is incomplete or the link to tax revenue is asserted rather than explained.

Emerging (1 mark): A simple relevant point such as 'fuel has inelastic demand' with no further development.

practice_questions.text: 'Price elasticity of supply is always more important than price elasticity of demand when a firm is deciding whether to expand production.' Evaluate this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Balanced evaluation that develops both sides. Arguments for the statement: PES tells the firm whether it can actually increase output when prices rise — if supply is inelastic (due to capacity constraints or long production times), expanding is difficult regardless of how strong demand is; in capital-intensive industries or where skilled labour is scarce, PES is the binding constraint. Arguments against: PED determines whether a price rise (or a decision to increase output and lower price) will be profitable — a firm expanding into a market with highly elastic demand may find prices fall sharply as output rises, wiping out the revenue gain. A good evaluation considers 'it depends on': the industry context (manufacturing vs services), the time horizon (short-run inelastic supply vs long-run elastic), and the specific decision (raising price vs entering a new market). Supported judgement that neither concept is universally more important — the right tool depends on the decision being made.

Secure (5–7 marks): Both sides developed with reasonable analysis. Judgement present but may lack clear supporting reasoning or context-specificity.

Developing (3–4 marks): Some discussion of both PES and PED but unbalanced — one side significantly weaker or the conclusion unsupported.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Simple points about what PED or PES means, with little or no attempt to evaluate.

knowledge_checks.q: What does a PED value of 2.5 (ignoring the sign) tell us about demand for that good?
options: Demand is price inelastic — quantity demanded changes less than proportionally to price
Demand is unit elastic — quantity demanded changes in exact proportion to price
Demand is price elastic — quantity demanded changes more than proportionally to price
Supply is price elastic — quantity supplied changes more than proportionally to price

knowledge_checks.q: A firm raises its price by 10% and total revenue increases. What does this tell us about the PED for its product?
options: PED is greater than 1 — demand is elastic
PED equals exactly 1 — demand is unit elastic
PED is less than 1 — demand is inelastic
PED is positive — supply and price move together

knowledge_checks.q: Price elasticity of demand is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in _____.
When a good has many close _____, its demand tends to be more price elastic because consumers can easily switch away if the price rises.
Match each elasticity concept to its correct description:
left: PES in the long run vs short run
right: Demand is elastic — a price rise causes a proportionally larger fall in quantity demanded
Demand is inelastic — a price rise causes a proportionally smaller fall in quantity demanded
Supply becomes more elastic over time as firms gain capacity and flexibility

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for price elasticity of demand?
flashcard_questions.a: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a PED value of 0.6 (ignoring the sign) tell you?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand is price inelastic — quantity demanded falls less than proportionally to a price rise.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a PED value of 1.8 (ignoring the sign) tell you?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand is price elastic — quantity demanded falls more than proportionally to a price rise.

flashcard_questions.q: If demand is inelastic and the firm raises its price, what happens to total revenue?
flashcard_questions.a: Total revenue rises, because the fall in quantity sold is smaller than the rise in price.

flashcard_questions.q: If demand is elastic and the firm raises its price, what happens to total revenue?
flashcard_questions.a: Total revenue falls, because the fall in quantity sold outweighs the higher price per unit.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does insulin have inelastic demand while designer trainers have elastic demand?
flashcard_questions.a: Insulin is a necessity with no substitute; designer trainers are a luxury with many alternatives.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does demand become more elastic over a longer time period?
flashcard_questions.a: Consumers find more substitutes and ways to adapt, so they respond more strongly to price changes.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for price elasticity of supply?
flashcard_questions.a: PES = % change in quantity supplied ÷ % change in price.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is PES always a positive number, while PED is always negative?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher prices incentivise more supply, so price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

flashcard_questions.q: A factory is running at full capacity. Is its supply elastic or inelastic in the short run?
flashcard_questions.a: Inelastic — it cannot quickly increase output because there is no spare capacity.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do governments tax petrol and tobacco heavily, using the logic of PED?
flashcard_questions.a: Demand is inelastic, so quantity sold barely falls after a tax, generating reliable revenue.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is supply in the long run almost always more elastic than in the short run?
flashcard_questions.a: Over time, firms can build new capacity, hire more workers, and find alternative resources — making it easier to increase output in response to a price rise.

flashcard_questions.q: What is 'total revenue', and how is it calculated?
flashcard_questions.a: The income a firm earns from sales; calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.

glossary_terms.definition: A measure of how much the quantity demanded of a good changes in response to a change in its price, calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
When the percentage change in quantity demanded is greater than the percentage change in price, so PED (ignoring the sign) is greater than 1.
When the percentage change in quantity demanded is less than the percentage change in price, so PED (ignoring the sign) is less than 1.
The income a firm receives from selling its output, calculated as price multiplied by quantity sold.
A measure of how much the quantity supplied of a good changes in response to a change in its price, calculated as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
The unused production potential that exists when a firm or economy is producing below its maximum possible output.
